And so I shall now withdraw from this retracing of its disposition, in order to complete the account of it. We define the soul as born of the breath of God, immortal, corporeal, shaped, simple in substance, knowing of itself, proceeding variously, free in will, subject to accidents, changeable through its faculties, rational, sovereign, divining, redundant out of one. It follows now that we consider how it is redundant out of one, that is, whence and when and by what reason it is taken up.

Some believe that they have come down from the heavens, with as much persuasion as they undoubtedly promise that they will return thither — as Saturninus, the disciple of Menander the Simonian, brought in, affirming that man was made by angels, and at first a feeble and weak and unstable work, throbbing on the earth like a worm, since the powers to stand were wanting; then, out of the mercy of the supreme power, to whose likeness, though not yet fully perceived, he had been rashly constructed, he obtained a little spark of life, which roused and erected him and animated him more steadily, and which after the departure of life is to be carried back to the mother-source. But Carpocrates too claims as much for himself out of the higher places, so that his disciples both equal their own souls now to Christ, let alone to the apostles, and, when they will, prefer them — souls which they have accordingly conceived out of a sublime virtue, despising the world's powerful principalities. Apelles relates that the souls were solicited by earthly baits, out of their supercelestial seats, by a fiery angel, the God of Israel and ours, who thereafter molded round them a sinful flesh. The school of Valentinus stuffs into the soul the seed of Sophia, through which they recognize the histories and Milesian tales of their Aeons out of the images of visible things. I grieve, in good faith, that Plato has been made the caterer of all the heretics. For it is his, in the Phaedo, that souls go thither from here and come hither from there. Likewise in the Timaeus, that the offspring of God, having had the generation of mortals delegated to them, when they had received the beginning of an immortal soul, froze about it a mortal body; and again that this world is the image of some other. All which, that he might commend it to belief — both that the soul, in former time in the higher places, lived with God in the fellowship of the Ideas, and that it crosses over hither from there, and that it here reviews the things it formerly knew of the exemplars — he elaborated a new argument, that ‘mathēseis’ are ‘anamnēseis,’ that is, that learnings are recollections. For souls, coming hither from there, forget the things in which they were before, and thereafter, taught by these visible things, remember. Since, then, by an argument of this kind those things are insinuated by Plato which the heretics borrow, I shall sufficiently strike the heretics back if I shatter the argument of Plato.

First, indeed, I shall not concede that the soul is capable of forgetting, because he has granted it so great a divinity that it is made equal to God. He makes it unborn, which alone I might have armed myself with for the testimony of full divinity; he adds immortal, incorruptible, incorporeal — for who has believed even God to be this? — invisible, unshapeable, uniform, principal, rational, intellectual. What more could he proscribe for the soul, if he called it God? But we, who attach nothing to God, by this very thing weigh the soul far below God, in that we acknowledge it to be born, and through this of a more diluted divinity and a slenderer felicity, as breath, not as spirit; and even if immortal, so that this is a matter of divinity, yet passible, so that this is a matter of birth, and therefore, from the very first origin, capable of straying, and thence too akin to forgetfulness. Enough of this with Hermogenes. But that which, so as to be deservedly held God out of the equalizing of all its properties, would lie subject to no passion, would also lie subject to no forgetfulness — since forgetfulness is as great an injury as is the glory of that of which it is the injury, namely memory, which Plato himself proclaimed the safety of the senses and the intellects, and Cicero the treasure-house of all studies. Nor is this now to be brought into doubt, whether so divine a soul could have lost its memory, but whether it can again recover what it has lost. For a thing which ought not to have forgotten, if it has forgotten, I know not whether it can remember. So both suit my soul, not Plato's. In the second place I shall object: Do you make the soul possessed of those Ideas by nature, or not? ‘By nature, surely,’ you say. No one, then, will grant that natural knowledge of natural arts can fall away. The knowledge of studies will fall away, of doctrines, of disciplines; perhaps too of talents and affections, which seem natural and yet are not — because, as we premised, they are constituted out of accidents, according to places and institutions and corporealities and states of health and presiding powers and freedoms of will. But the knowledge of natural things does not fail even in beasts. The lion will plainly forget his ferocity, when forestalled by the training of tameness, and with all his array of mane will become the darling of some queen Berenice, cleaning her cheeks with his tongue. Manners will leave the beast; the knowledge of natural things will remain. The same will not forget the natural foods, the natural remedies, the natural terrors; and even if the queen offer him fish, even if cakes, he will desire flesh; and if she compose theriac for him when ailing, the lion will require an ape; and if she set no hunting-spear against him, yet he will dread a cock. Just so for man too — perhaps the most forgetful of all — the knowledge of natural things alone, as alone natural, will persevere unobliterated: ever mindful of eating in hunger and drinking in thirst, and of what is to be seen with the eyes and heard with the ears and smelled with the nostrils and tasted with the mouth and handled with the hand. These are surely the senses, which philosophy depreciates by the preference of the intellectual. Therefore, if the natural knowledge of sensible things remains, how is it that the knowledge of intellectual things, which is held the superior, has perished? Whence now is the very force of forgetfulness that precedes recollection? ‘From the multitude of time,’ he says. Improvidently enough. For the quantity of time will not pertain to a thing said to be unborn, and through this above all believed eternal. For that which is eternal, in that it is unborn, admitting neither beginning nor end of time, suffers no measure of time. For that which has no measure of time is neither subject to time by any change, nor is there any force in it out of a multitude of time. If time is the cause of forgetfulness, why is it that, from the moment the soul is brought into the body, memory slips away, as though the soul thenceforth endures time — which without doubt was not prior to the body without time? But entering the body, does it at once forget, or some while after? If at once, what multitude of time, not yet to be reckoned, will there be? Infancy, namely. If some while after, then in that space, before the times of forgetfulness, will the soul still act mindful? And what kind of thing is it that afterwards it should forget, and again afterwards remember? But at whatever time forgetfulness rushes in upon it, how great a measure of time too will be reckoned here? The whole course of life, I suppose, will not be enough to overturn the memory of so great an age before the body. But again Plato changes the cause to the body, as though this too were worthy of belief, that a born substance should extinguish the power of an unborn one. But there are great and many differences of bodies, according to nationality, magnitude, habit, age, health. Will then differences of forgetfulnesses too be reckoned? But forgetfulness is uniform; therefore the multiform corporeality will not be the cause of a uniform result. Many proofs likewise, Plato himself being witness, have proved the divination of the soul, which we have already set forth to Hermogenes. But there is no one of men who does not himself at some time feel his soul to be foreseeing, the augur of an omen or a peril or a joy. If the body does not obstruct divination, neither, I suppose, will it stand in the way of memory. In the same body, certainly, souls both forget and remember. If some condition of the body strikes in forgetfulness, how will it admit recollection, which is its contrary? — since recollection itself too, after forgetfulness, is a memory revived. What is adverse to the first memory, why should it not also be repugnant to the second? Lastly, who would remember more than little children, as the more recent souls, as not yet plunged into domestic and public cares, as given over to their studies alone — whose learnings become recollections? Nay, why do we not all alike remember, since we all alike forget? But only the philosophers, you say. Not even all of these. Plato alone, namely, in so great a forest of nations, in so great a meadow of the wise, both forgot and remembered the Ideas. Therefore, if this chief argumentation in no way stands, the whole of that to which it was accommodated is equally overturned — that souls were to be believed unborn, and conversant in the heavens, and conscious there of divine things, and carried down from there, and here remembering — plainly to furnish occasions to the heretics.

Now then I shall return to the cause of this digression, to render how souls are redundant out of one — when, and where, and by what reason they are taken up. About which kind it matters nothing whether the question comes from a philosopher, or from a heretic, or from the common crowd. It makes no difference to the professors of truth about her adversaries, especially such bold ones as are, in the first place, those who presume that the soul is not conceived in the womb, nor compacted and produced together with the modeling of the flesh, but, when the birth has already been brought forth and the infant is not yet alive, is impressed upon it from without. Moreover, that the seed, sequestered from intercourse in the female parts and quickened by natural motion, thickens into the substance of flesh only; and that this, brought forth, and smoking from the furnace of the womb and loosened by heat, like iron made fiery and there plunged into cold water, so, struck by the rigour of the air, both seizes the animal power and gives back the sound of a voice. This the Stoics hold with Aenesidemus, and Plato himself at times, when he says that the soul, otherwise strange and an exile from the womb, is led in by the first inbreathing of the infant as it is born, just as it is led out by the last out-breathing. We shall see whether he has invented this opinion. Nor among the physicians too was Hicesius lacking, a prevaricator both of nature and of his own art. They were ashamed, I suppose, to lay down this which women would recognize. But how much more blushworthy an outcome, to be refuted by women than approved by them! For in this matter there is no master, arbiter, witness so suitable as the sex itself. Answer, you mothers — you who are pregnant, and you who have given birth — let the barren and the males be silent; the truth of your nature is inquired into, the faith of your experience is convened. Do you perceive in the fetus any vital movement other than your own, by which the loins throb, the sides quiver, the whole compass of the belly is pulsed, the whole region of the burden shifts? Are these motions your joys and your sure security, that you so confide the infant both to live and to play? Or, if its restlessness ceases, do you fear for it first? Does it even now hear within you, when it is startled at a new sound? Do you even crave food-fancies for it, and even feel loathings for it? Do you even share your states of health with each other — it indeed even out of your bruises, by which it too within is marked through the same members, snatching to itself its mother's injuries? If livid bruise and redness is a passion of the blood, there will be no blood without a soul; if illness is an access of the soul, there will be no illness without a soul; if nourishment, fasting, increases, decreases, fear, motion are a handling of the soul, then he who exercises these will live. In short, he ceases to live who ceases to exercise them. In short, the dead too are brought forth — how, unless they too were once alive? And who are even the dead, unless those who were first alive? But indeed even in the very womb the infant is slaughtered by a necessary cruelty, when in the delivery, turned aslant, it denies the birth — a matricide, unless it is to die. And so among the instruments of physicians there is even an organ by which the secret parts are first compelled to open, with a screw-fitted apparatus; with a ring-knife, by which the members within are cut up by an anxious decision; with a blunt hook, by which the whole deed is drawn out by a violent delivery. There is also a brazen spike, by which the very throat-cutting is directed in a blind brigandage: they call it the ‘embryo-slayer,’ from the office of infanticide, the destroyer, assuredly, of a living infant. This both Hippocrates had, and Asclepiades, and Erasistratus, and Herophilus too, dissector even of grown men, and the gentler Soranus himself — all certain that a living creature is conceived, and so, taking pity on so most unhappy an infancy of this kind, that it should be killed first, lest it be torn alive. Of which necessity of crime Hicesius too, I believe, did not doubt, while he superadds the soul to those already born from the stroke of cold air — since even the very word for soul among the Greeks answers to a cooling. Are then the barbarian and Roman nations animated otherwise, because they have named the soul by something other than ‘psychē’? And how many nations are reckoned under the most blazing pole, scorched even in their colour? Whence have they a soul, who have no rigour of air? I say nothing of the heat of bed-chambers and all the apparatus of warmth necessary there for women in labour, to be exposed to whose breath of air is rather a danger. In the very baths almost the fetus slips out, and at once the wail is heard. For the rest, if the rigour of air is the treasure of the soul, then outside the Germanies and Scythias and the Alps and the Argaean ranges no one ought to be born. And yet the peoples are more frequent in the eastern and southern temperature, and the talents more nimble, while all the Sarmatians too are torpid in mind. For minds, too, would come forth wiser out of rigours, if souls came out of little chills, since the power is together with the substance. These things being thus established beforehand, we can also call to mind those too who, drawn alive from their mother's womb cut open, drank the air — certain men named Liber and Scipio. But if anyone, like Plato, thinks accordingly that two souls cannot come together into one, just as neither can two bodies — to him I would show not only two souls heaped together into one, as also two bodies, in fetuses, but many other things too joined with the soul, namely a demon, and not one only, as in Socrates himself, but even of a sevenfold spirit, as in Magdalene, and of a legionary number, as in the Gerasene — so that the more easily soul will be joined with soul out of community of substance than an evil spirit out of diversity of nature. But the same man, in the sixth book of the Laws, admonishing us to beware lest the corruption of the seed, from some baseness of intercourse, should breed a blemish for body and soul, has, I know not, slipped more from his earlier or from this opinion. For he shows that the soul is brought in from the seed, which he warns must be cared for — not from the first inbreathing of the one born. Whence, I ask you, do we answer the likeness of the soul too to our parents in our talents, according to the testimony of Cleanthes, if we are not also brought out from the soul's seed? And why did even the ancient astrologers reckon a man's nativity from the beginning of conception, if from that point the soul too is not there? To which equally pertains, if anything does, the breath.

But all the unevenness of human opinion reaches only as far as the boundaries of God. To our own lines now I shall gather my step, that what I have answered to the philosophers and physicians I may prove to the Christian. Build your faith, brother, on your own foundation. Look upon the living wombs of the most holy women, with the infants there not merely already breathing, but even prophesying. Behold, the bowels of Rebecca are disquieted, and the birth is still far off, and there is no impulse of air; behold, the twofold fetus tumultuates in the mother's parts, and there are nowhere as yet two peoples. A portentous petulance, perhaps, of an infancy contending before it lives, spirited before it is animated — if only it had troubled its mother by leaping. But when the birth is opened, and the number is inspected, and what was augured is recognized, then, I think, not only the souls of the infants are proved, but their battles too. He who had come first to be born was held back by the one forestalled, not yet more fully brought forth, but only born as to the hand. And if the first was drinking in his soul from the first inbreathing in the Platonic manner, or plucking it from the rigour of the air in the Stoic fashion, what of that one who was awaited, who was still detained within and already detaining the other without? Not yet breathing, I suppose, he had assailed his brother's heel; still hot with his mother, he desired to come forth before him. O infant both rival and strong and already contentious — alive, I believe! Look too upon singular conceptions, and indeed more monstrous ones, of the barren and of the virgin, who by this very thing might have brought forth imperfect ones, for the overthrowing of nature — since the one was numb to the seed, the other untouched. It were fitting, if anything, that those should be born without a soul who had not been duly conceived; but they too live, each in its own womb. Elizabeth exults — John had struck within; Mary glorifies the Lord — Christ had moved within. The mothers recognize each their own fetuses, themselves recognized in turn by them — assuredly living ones, which were not only souls, but spirits too. So too you read the voice of God to Jeremiah: ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.’ If God forms in the womb, He also breathes in, after the manner of the first origin: ‘And God formed man, and breathed into him the breath of life.’ Nor would God know man in the womb unless whole: ‘And before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you.’ And a body still dead? By no means whatever. For God is the God of the living, not of the dead.

How then is the living creature conceived? Is the substance of both body and soul fused together at once, or does one of them precede? Nay, we say that both are at once conceived, and formed, and perfected, just as they are also brought forth; nor does any interval come in within the conception, by which an order might be arranged. For reconsider the first things from the last. If death is determined to be nothing other than the disjunction of body and soul, life, the contrary of death, will be defined as nothing other than the conjunction of body and soul. If the disjunction befalls both substances at once through death, this ought to be the form which conjunction too, equally befalling both substances through life, has dictated. Now we acknowledge life from conception, since we claim the soul from conception; for from that point life exists at which the soul does. Equally, therefore, those things are compacted into life which are equally separated in death. Then, if we give the primacy to one and the second place to the other, the times of the seed too must be distinguished according to the order of their rank. And when will the seed of the body be deposited, when that of the soul? Nay, if the times of the seeds are divided, then diverse materials too will be held, out of the distance of the times. For even though we shall confess two species of seed, the corporeal and the animal, yet we claim them to be undistinguished, and in this way contemporaneous and of the same moment. Let us therefore not be ashamed of a necessary interpretation. Nature is to be revered, not to be blushed at. It is lust, not the act, that has befouled intercourse; it is the excess, not the institution, that is unchaste, since the institution is blessed by God: ‘Increase and abound into a multitude.’ But the excess is cursed — adulteries and stuprations and brothels. In this solemn office of the sexes, then, which mingles male and female — in common intercourse, I mean — we know that both soul and flesh perform their function together, the soul by concupiscence, the flesh by act, the soul by instinct, the flesh by the deed. By a single impulse of both, then, the whole man being shaken, the seed of the whole man is foamed out, having from the corporeal substance its moisture, from the animal its warmth. And if the soul is a cold thing in the name the Greeks give it, why does the body grow cold when it is removed? In short — that I may now risk myself more by modesty than by proof — in that very heat of the last pleasure, by which the genital fluid is expelled, do we not perceive that something of the soul too goes out? And do we not accordingly grow faint and feeble, with a loss of light? This will be the animal seed, straightway from the distillation of the soul, just as that corporeal fluid too is the seed from the purging of the flesh. Most faithful are the examples of the first origin. From clay was the flesh in Adam. What else is clay than a rich liquid? Thence will be the genital fluid. From the inbreathing of God was the soul. What else is the inbreathing of God than a vapour of the spirit? Thence will be that which we exhale through that fluid. Since therefore in the first origin two diverse and divided things, clay and breath, had been compacted into one man, the two substances, now confused into one, mixed their own seeds too, and thence handed down a form for propagating the race; so that even now the two, though diverse, even united, flow forth equally, and equally insinuated into their furrow and field, equally make man bud forth out of both substances; in whom again its own seed is inborn after its kind, just as it has been prefixed for every generative condition. Therefore from one man comes all this redundancy of souls — nature, namely, observing the edict of God: ‘Increase and abound into a multitude.’ For even in the very preface of His one work, ‘Let us make man,’ the whole posterity was foretold in the plural: ‘And let them have dominion over the fishes of the sea.’ No wonder: the promise of the harvest is in the seed.

What now is that old saying in the memory of Plato about the reciprocal coursing of souls — that those departing hence go thither, and again come hither and live, and thence depart from life, and again out of the dead are made alive? Pythagorean, as some will have it; divine, Albinus thinks it, of the Egyptian Mercury perhaps. But there is no divine saying except of the one God, with which the prophets, with which the apostles, with which Christ Himself thundered. Moses, much more ancient even than Saturn by about nine hundred years — let alone than his great-grandsons — and certainly much more divine, who set forth the descents of the human race from the beginning of the world too, through the several births, by name and by time, sufficiently proving the divinity of the work out of the divination of his utterance. But if the Samian sophist is Plato's authority concerning the relapse of souls, ever rolled back out of the alternate substitution of dead and living, certainly that Pythagoras, though good in other respects, yet, in order to build up this opinion, leaned upon a lie not only base but even rash. Learn, you who do not know, and believe with us. He feigns death, hides in an underground place, there condemns himself to seven years' endurance; meanwhile he learns from his only confidant and minister, his mother, those things concerning the recently dead which he was to relate for the credit of the matter; and when he has seemed to himself to have falsified his corporeality sufficiently for all the horror of an old corpse, he emerges from the recesses of his deceit, as one given back from the dead. Who would not believe that he whom he had believed dead had come to life again, hearing especially from him those things about the dead posterity which he could not seem to have learned except among the dead? So that the living are made out of the dead is an older saying. What of it, if it were even younger? Neither does truth desire antiquity, nor does falsehood shun novelty. I hold it plainly false, though noble in age; why not false, whose testimony too is from falsehood? How shall I believe that Pythagoras does not lie, who lies that I may believe? How will he persuade me that he was Aethalides and Euphorbus and Pyrrhus the fisherman and Hermotimus, before Pythagoras, in order to persuade me that the living are made out of the dead — he who again perjured himself to be Pythagoras? For by as much as it would have been more credible that he himself had once returned into life out of himself, than so often one and then another — by so much, in the harder matter, did he deceive, who lied in the softer. But he recognized the shield of Euphorbus once consecrated at Delphi, and said it was his own, and proved it by marks commonly unknown. Look to his underground vault, and, if it suffices, believe. For one who contrived such a trick, with injury to his good health, with the fraud of a life racked for seven years beneath the earth by fasting, sloth, and shadow — to whom the loathing of the sky was of such worth — what rashness would he not have approached, what curiosity would he not have attempted, to arrive at the mark of that shield? But what, if he found it in some more hidden histories? What, if he drank in some surviving little breaths of fame of a now decayed tradition? What, if, bribing the temple-keeper, he learned it by a secret inspection? We know too that it is permitted to magic to explore hidden things through the spirits of the underworld and the familiars and the Pythonic ones. For did not even Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras, perhaps divine — not to say dream — by these arts? What, if the same demon was in him who in Euphorbus too had done the deeds of blood? In short, he who had proved himself Euphorbus from the argument of the shield, why did he recognize none of the Trojans, his fellow-soldiers, in like manner? For they too would by now have come to life again, if the living were made out of the dead.

That the dead are made out of the living is established; yet not on that account also the living out of the dead. For from the beginning the living were prior; whence from the beginning equally the dead were posterior — from nowhere else than from the living. The former had something whence they might rather arise, provided it was not from the dead; the latter had nothing whence they could rather be derived, except from the living. Therefore, if from the beginning the living were not from the dead, why afterwards from the dead? Had that fount of origin, whatever it is, failed? Or did the form repent? And how is it preserved in the dead? Is it not the case that, because from the beginning the dead were from the living, therefore always from the living? For either in both directions the form of the beginning would have persevered, or in both it would have changed; so that, if afterwards the living ought to be made out of the dead, equally it ought also that the dead should be made not out of the living. If the faith of the institution were not to be equalized, contraries are not everywhere reformed by alternation out of contraries. For we too shall set against them the contrarieties of the born and the unborn, of sight and blindness, of youth and age, of wisdom and folly; and yet the unborn does not therefore come from the born because a contrary is made out of a contrary, nor sight again out of blindness because blindness befalls out of sight, nor youth revive again out of age because age withers out of youth, nor folly become blunted again out of wisdom because wisdom is sharpened out of folly. These things Albinus too, fearing for his Plato, subtly inquires into, distinguishing the kinds of contrarieties — as though these too were not as absolutely placed among contrarieties as those which are interpreted toward the opinion of his master, life, I mean, and death. And yet life is not given back out of death because death is brought down out of life.

But what shall we answer to the rest? First, if the living are from the dead, as the dead are from the living, then one and altogether the same number of all men would have stuck fast forever — that number, namely, which had first entered upon life. For the living are prior to the dead, then the dead out of the living, and again the living out of the dead. And while this is always out of the same, so always there would be just as many as are out of the same. For neither would more or fewer have gone out than had returned. But we find, even in the Commentaries on Human Antiquities, that the human race has gradually grown beyond measure, while the Aborigines, or wanderers, or exiles, or any glory-seekers occupy lands — as the Scythians occupied the Parthian lands, as the Temenidae the Peloponnese, as the Athenians Asia, as the Phrygians Italy and the Phoenicians Africa — while there are also solemn migrations, which they call colonies, by counsel of unburdening the population, vomiting forth swarms of a nation into other territories. For the Aborigines now both remain in their own seats and have lent out their stock elsewhere in greater measure. Certainly the very world is plain to see, more cultivated by the day and better furnished than of old. All places are now traversed, all are known, all are busy with commerce; most charming farms have blotted out the once notorious wildernesses, fields have tamed the woods, flocks have put to flight the wild beasts, the sands are sown, the rocks are planted, the marshes are drained, there are as many cities as there were once cottages. No longer do the islands fright, nor the crags terrify; everywhere a house, everywhere a people, everywhere a commonwealth, everywhere life. The greatest testimony of human frequency: we are burdensome to the world, the elements scarcely suffice us, our necessities are sharper, and complaints are on the lips of all, while now nature does not sustain us. In truth, pestilence and famine and wars and the engulfings of cities are to be reckoned as a remedy, like a pruning of the human race grown overgrown. And yet, when axes of this kind cut down the greatest force of mortals at one stroke, the world has never once, after a thousand years, been frightened at its restitution, bringing the living back out of the dead. For an equal force of loss and of restitution would have made this too perceptible, if the living were made out of the dead. But why a thousand years after, and not at once the living out of the dead — since, if what was paid out were not at once made up, it would be endangered to be wholly consumed, the defect forestalling the restitution, because this furlough of life would not pay back the equivalent of the millennial period, being far shorter and therefore more easily extinguished before being rekindled? Therefore that which in this way would have perished, if the living were made out of the dead — when it has not perished — it will not be credible that the living are made out of the dead.

Now indeed, if the living are from the dead, then assuredly single ones from single ones. The souls of single bodies, therefore, ought to have returned, as single, into single bodies. Moreover, if even two and three and five at a time are resumed in one womb, the living will not be from the dead, since they are not single from single. And in this way too the form of the first origin is marked, since even now several souls are brought forth from one. Likewise, since souls depart at various ages, why do they return at one age? For all are imbued from infancy. But what kind of thing is it that an old man, deceased, should return an infant? If the soul decreases without, retrograding in age, how much more was it fit that it should return more advanced after a thousand years? Or at least coeval with its own death, so as to recover again the age it had left. But even if the same souls were always rolled round, although not the same forms of bodies too, yet they ought at least to carry back with them the former properties of talents and studies and affections, since otherwise they would rashly be held the same, lacking those things by which the same would be proved. ‘How do you know,’ you say, ‘whether it does not indeed happen so, secretly, but the condition of the millennial age destroys the faculty of recognizing, because they return unknown to you?’ But I know it does not happen so, since you set Pythagoras-Euphorbus against me. For behold, it is sufficiently established that Euphorbus was a military and warlike soul, even from the very glory of the consecrated shields; but Pythagoras so inactive and unwarlike that, shunning the battles of Greece then, he preferred the quiet of Italy, devoted to geometry and astrology and music, a stranger to the study and affection of Euphorbus. But Pyrrhus too occupied himself in catching fishes; Pythagoras, on the contrary, not even in eating them, abstaining as from living creatures. Aethalides, moreover, and Hermotimus had even thrust the bean into the common foods; but Pythagoras handed it down to his disciples that one was not even to pass through a bean-field. How then are the same souls recovered, which will be proved the same neither by talents nor by institutions nor now by foods? Now then, out of so great a census of Greece, four souls only are reckoned. But why at all of the census of Greece alone, and not out of every nation, and out of every age and dignity, and lastly out of every sex — since transmigrations and transincorporations come about daily — why does Pythagoras alone recognize himself as one and then another, and not I too? Or if it is the privilege of philosophers, and assuredly of Greeks — as though Scythians and Indians too did not philosophize — why does Epicurus remember himself as no one before, Chrysippus as no one, Zeno as no one, not even Plato himself, whom perhaps we would have believed Nestor on account of the honey of his eloquence?

But indeed Empedocles, who had raved himself a god, therefore, I suppose, disdaining to remember himself any hero, says, ‘I was a bush and a fish.’ Why not rather a pumpkin too, so insipid, and a chameleon, so puffed up? Plainly, as a fish, that he might not rot in some more decent burial, he chose rather to be roasted by hurling himself into Aetna. And thereupon let metempsychosis have ended in him, like a summer supper after the roast. Accordingly here too we must needs contend against a yet more portentous presumption, which revolves beasts out of men and men out of beasts. Let the bushes look to it. I shall be allowed to be brief too, lest I be compelled to laugh more than to teach. We say that the human soul can in no way be transferred into beasts, even if, according to the philosophers, it were reckoned from elemental substances. For whether the soul be fire, or water, or blood, or breath, or air, or light, we ought to reconsider the animals contrary to each of the several species: to fire, those that are cold, the snakes, lizards, salamanders, and whatever is produced from the rival element, namely from water; likewise contrary to water, those that are dry and juiceless — in short, locusts, little butterflies, chameleons rejoice in dryness; likewise contrary to blood, those that lack its purple — snails, little worms, and the greater census of fishes; but contrary to breath, those that do not seem to breathe, lacking lungs and arteries — gnats, ants, moths, and this kind of little creatures; likewise contrary to air, those living things which, ever living underground and underwater, lack the drawing-in of it (you would know the things rather than the names); likewise contrary to light, those that are wholly blind, or have eyes only for the darkness — moles, bats, owls. These things, that I may teach from substances apparent and manifest. But if I were to hold the atoms of Epicurus, and to see the numbers of Pythagoras, and to come upon the Ideas of Plato, and to seize the entelechies of Aristotle, I should perhaps find, even for these species, animals which I might oppose by the name of contrariety. For I contend that, out of whatever substance above-named the human soul might have consisted, it could not have been reformed into animals so contrary to each several substance, and confer upon them a census from its own transference — by which it would rather have to be excluded and rejected than admitted and received under the name of this first contrariety, which makes a diversity of substantial state, and then the rest too, by the consequent order of each nature. For the human soul has been allotted other seats, and ways of feeding, and equipment, and senses, and affections, and modes of intercourse, and offspring; likewise talents, then works, joys, weariness, vices, desires, pleasures, states of health, medicines; and lastly its own ways of life too and exits of death. How then will that soul which clung to the earth, fearless of no height, of no depth, weary even at climbing stairs, suffocated even by plunging into pools, afterwards insult the air in an eagle, or afterwards leap into the sea in an eel? How likewise, brought up on liberal and dainty and well-tended foods, will it chew — I do not say chaff, but thorns and the wild bitternesses of leaves, and the beasts of dunghills, and even the venoms of worms — if it pass into a goat, or into a quail, or even into carrion, even into human flesh, mindful surely of itself in a bear or a lion? So you will reduce the rest too to incongruity, that we may not delay over pleading each. Whatever measure the human soul itself has, whatever its size, what will it do in animals far larger or far smaller? For of necessity both every body is filled by a soul, and every soul covered by a body. How then will the soul of a man fill an elephant? How likewise will it be covered in a gnat? If it is so far extended or contracted, it will surely be endangered. And therefore I add: if it is in no way capable of such a transference into animals not corresponding to it either in the measures of their bodies or in the other laws of its own nature — will it then be changed according to the qualities of the kinds and their life contrary to human life, itself too made contrary to the human by change? But in fact, if it admits of change, losing what it was, it will not be what it was; and if it will not be what it was, metempsychosis is dissolved — not to be ascribed, namely, to that soul which, if it will be changed, will not be. For it would be called metempsychosis of whatever soul would suffer it while remaining in its own state. Therefore, if it can neither be changed, lest it be not itself, nor remain in its state, since it does not admit contraries — I still seek some cause worthy of belief for a transference of this kind. For even though certain men are equated to beasts according to the qualities of their characters and talents and affections — since God too says, ‘Man, when he was in honour, was likened to the irrational beasts’ — yet kites are not therefore made out of the rapacious, and dogs out of the filthy, and panthers out of the cruel, or sheep out of the honest, and swallows out of the chattering, and doves out of the chaste, as though the same substance of soul everywhere repeated its nature in the properties of animals. But substance is one thing, and the nature of substance another; since substance is proper to each thing, but nature can be common. Take an example. Stone is a substance, iron is a substance; the hardness of stone and iron is the nature of the substance. The hardness they share; in substance they disagree. The softness of wool, the softness of feather — let their natural properties pair them off, their substantial ones do not pair them. So too, if a savage or an honest man be called a beast, yet it is not the same soul. For then too the likeness of nature is noted when the unlikeness of substance is observed. For the very fact that you judge a man like a beast, you confess the soul not the same, by saying ‘like,’ not ‘the very same.’ So the divine pronouncement too is wise, equating man to the cattle in nature, not in substance. For neither would God have marked man in this way, if He knew him a beast in substance.

Even when this dogma is claimed under the name of judgment — that human souls are allotted kinds of animals according to their life and merits, some to be slaughtered in the slaughterhouses, some to be broken in for servile uses, some to be wearied in labours, some to be fouled among the unclean; and accordingly to be honoured and loved and tended and sought after in the fairest and most upright and most useful and daintiest — here too I will say: if they are changed, the very souls that will have earned will not be requited, and the principle of judgment will be voided, if the sense of merits be lacking. But the sense of merits will be lacking, if the state of the souls be turned; and the state of the souls is turned, if they have not persevered the same. Equally, if they will persevere unto judgment — which even the Egyptian Mercury knew, saying that the soul, departed from the body, is not refunded into the soul of the universe, but remains determinate, ‘that it may render an account,’ he says, ‘to the Father of the things it did in the body’ — I wish, assuredly, to review the justice, the gravity, the majesty, the dignity of the divine judgment, whether human censure does not preside at a more sublime height, fuller of the honour of both sentences, of punishments and of rewards, severer in avenging and more liberal in bestowing. What do you think the soul of a murderer will become? Some beast, I suppose, destined for the butchery and the meat-market, that it may likewise be slaughtered, because it too slaughtered; likewise be flayed, because it too despoiled; likewise be set out for food, because it too cast to the beasts those whom it butchered in woods and pathless places. If it shall be so judged, will not that soul bring back more solace than punishment, in that it finds its funeral among the most precious cooks, in that it is buried with the spices of an Apicius and a Lurco, in that it is brought in on Ciceronian tables, in that it is borne out on the most splendid platters of the Sullae, in that it suffers a banquet for its obsequies, in that it is devoured by its equals rather than by kites and wolves — so that, entombed in a man's body and returned to its own kind, it might seem to have risen again, exulting against human judgments, if it had experienced them? For human judgments rend the assassin with various and exquisite and now unnaturally trained beasts, and indeed while living — nay, while not easily dying, the end being delayed of set purpose, to the fullness of the penalty. But even if the soul has fled before the final sword, lest the body too should escape the iron, nonetheless, the throat and belly being run through and the ribs transfixed, requital is exacted for its own crime. Thence it is given to the fire, that even its burial may be a punishment. Otherwise, in short, it is not permitted. Nor yet is so much care taken of the pyre that other beasts may find the remains; certainly neither are the bones spared, nor are the ashes indulged with being left to lie bare. So great among men is the vengeance for murder as is the very nature that is avenged. Who would not prefer the justice of the age, which the apostle too testifies is not armed with the sword in vain, which is religiously stern in the cause of man? If we consider too the wages of the other crimes — the gibbets and the burnings alive and the sacks and the hooks and the crags — for whom would it not be expedient to suffer the sentence of Pythagoras and Empedocles? For even those who are to be punished with labours and servitudes, and are to be re-embodied surely into asses and mules, how they will congratulate themselves on the mills and the water-wheels, if they remember the mines and the workhouses and the public works and the very prisons, idle though these may be! Likewise, of those who, having behaved uprightly, have commended their life to the Judge, I seek rewards, but rather find punishments. Doubtless it is a great reward to the good, to be restored into animals of whatever kind. Homer remembered that he had been a peacock, when Ennius dreamed it; but I will not believe the poets even when they are awake. Even if the peacock is most beautiful, and most adorned with whatever colour it will — yet its feathers are silent, its voice displeases, and the poets would rather do nothing else than sing. Homer therefore was condemned into a peacock, not honoured. He will rejoice more in the world's remuneration, accounted the father of the liberal disciplines, so that he prefers the ornaments of his fame to those of a tail. Come now: granting that the poets pass into peacocks or into swans — if there is a comely voice even to swans — what animal will you put upon a just man, an Aeacus? What beast upon a chaste woman, a Dido? What bird will patience, what beast will sanctity, what fish will innocence be allotted? All things are the servants of man, all subjected, all his chattels. If he is to be any of these, he is diminished there, he to whom, for the merits of his life, images, statues and inscriptions, public honours, privileges are repaid; for whom the senate, for whom the people offer sacrifice with their votes. O divine judgments after death, more lying than human ones! contemptible as to penalties, despicable as to favours, which neither the worst will fear nor the best desire, to which the wicked rather than the holy will hasten — those, that they may the sooner escape the justice of the age, these, that they may the later attain it! Well do you philosophers teach, profitably do you persuade, that the punishments or rewards after death are lighter; whereas, if any judgment awaits souls, it ought to be believed heavier in the requital of life than in its administration, since nothing is fuller than what is final, and nothing fuller than what is more divine. God therefore will judge more fully, because more finally, by an eternal sentence both of punishment and of refreshment, the souls returning not into beasts, but into their own bodies. And this once, and on that day which the Father alone knows, that by a suspended expectation the solicitude of faith may be proved, ever watching for the day while ever ignorant of it, fearing daily what it daily hopes.

No opinion of this kind of madness, indeed, has to this day broken forth under a heretical name, refashioning human souls into beasts. But we have necessarily brought in and excluded this species too, as cohering with the foregoing, so that just as Euphorbus was beaten back in Pythagoras, so Homer might be beaten back in the peacock; and thus, this metempsychosis or metensomatosis also being repelled, that other might again be cut down which furnished something to the heretics. For Simon of Samaria too, in the Acts of the Apostles, the would-be purchaser of the Holy Spirit — after, being condemned by him, he had wept in vain over his destruction together with his money — turned to the assault of the truth, as if by way of solace for his revenge; and, supported also by the powers of his art, for the deceptions of some virtue, he redeemed with that same money a certain Helen of Tyre out of a place of public lust, a worthy wage for himself in place of the Holy Spirit. And he feigns himself indeed the supreme Father, but her his first conception, by which he had conceived to found angels and archangels; that she, possessed of this design, leapt forth from the Father and bounded down into the lower regions, and there, forestalling the Father's design, brought forth the angelic powers, ignorant of the Father, the artificer of this world; that by these, out of an equal mind, she was thence detained, lest, if she departed, they should seem the offspring of another, and was therefore consigned to every contumely, so that, cheapened, she might nowhere be free to depart; that she fell down even to human form, to be coerced as it were by the chains of the flesh. So, rolled through many ages in one and another womanly habit, she was even that Helen so destructive to Priam, and afterwards to the eyes of Stesichorus, whom she had both blinded for the abuse of his song and afterwards given back their light for the satisfaction of his praise; and so, migrating from bodies into bodies, in a last disgrace, under the title of prostitution she stood for hire, a viler Helen. This, then, is the lost sheep, to whom the supreme Father descended — Simon, namely; and, having first recovered and carried her back, on his shoulders or his thighs I know not, thereafter looked to the salvation of men, as by way of vengeance for those to be freed from those angelic powers — for whose deceiving he too, equally configured, and falsely pretending to be a man among men, played in Judaea the Son, but in Samaria the Father. O Helen, toiling between the poets and the heretics, infamous now for adultery, now for stuprum! — except that it is more gloriously that she is rescued out of Troy than out of a brothel: from Troy by a thousand ships, from the brothel perhaps not by a thousand denarii. Blush, Simon, slower in seeking, more inconstant in drawing back. But Menelaus at once pursues the lost one, at once demands back the snatched one, wrings her out by a ten years' war, not lurking, not deceiving, not given to caviling. I fear that he was rather the Father, who laboured about the recovery of Helen both more vigilantly and more boldly and longer.

But not for you alone did metempsychosis frame this fable. From it Carpocrates too uses it, alike a magus, alike a fornicator, save that he has less of a Helen. Why not, when he asserted that souls are re-embodied for the establishing of an utter overthrow of divine and human discipline? For he holds that this life is made firm to no one unless all the things that arraign it have been wiped out, since a thing is held evil not by nature but by opinion; and so metempsychosis necessarily impends, if in this very first journey of life satisfaction is not made for all things forbidden. To wit, crimes are assigned to life. For the rest, the soul has to be recalled as often as it has discharged anything too little, a debtor for its faults, until it pays the last farthing, thrust again and again into the prison of the body. For to this he adapts that whole allegory of the Lord, which shines forth with certain interpretations, and is first to be understood simply. For the heathen man too is our adversary, walking in the same way of common life. For the rest, we should have to go out of the world, if we might not converse with such. He bids you, then, show goodness of mind toward him. ‘For love your enemies,’ He says, ‘and pray for those who curse you,’ lest, provoked by injury through some dealing of business, he drag you off to his judge, and you, handed over into custody, be tortured to the payment of the whole debt. Then, if the mention of the adversary is transferred to the devil, you are warned, by the attendant observance, to enter into concord with him too, which is reckoned from the covenant of the faith; for you have agreed to renounce both him and his pomp and his angels. It is agreed between you on this point. This will be the friendship of the observance of the pledge, that you take nothing of his afterwards from those things which you have abjured, which you have rendered back to him — lest he charge you before God the Judge as a defrauder, as a transgressor of the pact, even as we read of him elsewhere as the accuser of the saints and the informer concerning his very name; and the judge deliver you to the angel of execution, and he consign you to the infernal prison, whence you shall not be dismissed until even the smallest fault be expended by the delay of the resurrection. What is fitter than these senses? What is truer than these interpretations? For the rest, with Carpocrates, if the soul is the debtor of all crimes, who is to be understood as its enemy and adversary? The better mind, I believe, which has driven it into some act of innocence, to be forced again and again into the body, until it be found guilty in nothing of a good life. This is to recognize the good tree from its evil fruits — that is, to acknowledge the doctrine of truth from the worst precepts. I suspect that heretics of this kind seize upon the example of Elias too, as represented thus in John, so that the Lord's pronouncement should patronize metempsychosis: ‘Elias has already come, and they knew him not’; and elsewhere, ‘And if you will receive it, this is Elias who is to come.’ Did the Jews, then, ask John out of the Pythagorean opinion, ‘Are you Elias?’ — and not out of the divine preaching, ‘And behold, I will send you Elias the Tishbite’? But indeed their metempsychosis is the recall of a soul long since dead and repeated into another body. Elias, however, is to come not from any departure of life, but from a translation; nor to be restored to a body from which he was not removed, but to be given back to the world from which he was translated; not out of any return from exile of life, but out of a supplement of prophecy — the same both himself, and of his own name and of his own person. But how is Elias John? You have the angel's word: ‘And he himself,’ he says, ‘shall go before the people in the power and in the spirit of Elias’ — not in his soul nor in his flesh. For these substances are each man's own. But spirit and power are conferred from without, out of the grace of God; and so they can be transferred into another, by the will of God, as was done formerly with the spirit of Moses.

Into these questions we digressed thence, I think, whither we must now return. We had laid down that the soul is sown in man himself and out of him, and that there is one seed from the first origin — as of the flesh too unto the whole census of the race — namely on account of the rival opinions of philosophers and heretics, and that drowsy saying of Plato. Now we weave the order of the treatises that follow thereupon. The soul, sown in the womb together with the flesh, is allotted its sex together with it, equally so, in such a way that in the cause of sex neither substance is held responsible. For if, in the seeds of the two substances, their conception admitted any interval, so that either the flesh or the soul were sown first, there would be ground for ascribing the property of sex to one substance by reason of the temporal interval of the seeds, so that either the flesh should engrave its sex upon the soul, or the soul upon the flesh; since Apelles too — not the painter, but the heretic — by setting up souls, male and female, before bodies, as he learned from Philumene, assuredly makes the flesh, as the later, receive its sex from the soul. And those who superinduce the soul upon the flesh after birth, assuredly pre-judge for the soul the male or female sex of the flesh already formed. But the undistinguished seeds of both substances and the united effusion of them undergo the common outcome of the kind, in whatever direction that account of nature, whatever it be, has drawn its lines. Certainly here too the form of the first origin attests itself, since the male is shaped earlier — for Adam was first; the female somewhat later — for Eve was after. So for a long while the flesh is unformed, such as it was plucked from Adam's side; yet it too was already a living creature even then, for I would acknowledge even that portion of Adam to have been a soul. For the rest, the inbreathing of God would have animated it too, had it not been that, as of flesh, so of soul too, there had been a tradux from Adam into the woman.

But every equipment of sowing, building, fashioning man in the womb is regulated by some power, the minister of the divine will, allotted to set in motion whatever account it does. By estimating this, even Roman superstition feigned a goddess Alemona for nourishing the fetus in the womb, and Nona and Decima from the more anxious months, and Partula, who governs the birth, and Lucina, who brings into the light. But we believe the divine offices to be angels. Therefore the fetus in the womb is a man from the point at which the form is completed. For the law of Moses too then judges the abortion guilty of retribution, when it is already the case of a man, when there is already reckoned to it a status of life and death, when it is already enrolled even under fate, even though, while still living in the mother, it shares most of its lot with the mother. I will say something too of the times of the soul's being born, that I may run through the order. The lawful birth is generally the entrance of the tenth month. Those who reason about numbers both venerate the number ten as thence the parent of the rest, and, in short, as the perfecter of human nativity. But I will rather argue this measure of time toward God, that the ten months should rather inaugurate man by the Decalogue — that we should be born in as great a number of time as we are reborn by the number of the discipline. But also, since at the seventh month the birth is complete, more easily than at the eighth, I shall recognize the honour of the sabbath, so that on the day on which the creation of God was dedicated, in that month the image of God should sometimes be brought forth. It is granted to the birth to hasten, and yet to fall fitly upon the hebdomad, into the auspices of resurrection and of rest and of the kingdom. Therefore the eighth does not create us; for then there will be no marriages. The fellowship of flesh and soul we long since commended, from the joining of their very seeds even to the perfection of the modeling. Likewise now we defend it from birth too, first of all in that they grow together, but by a different account according to the condition of their kinds, the flesh by measure, the soul by talent, the flesh by habit, the soul by sense. But it is to be denied that the soul grows in substance, lest it be also said to decrease in substance, and so be believed even destined to fail; but its power, in which the natural endowments are kept implanted, is gradually brought forth with the flesh, the measure of its substance being preserved, with which it was breathed in from the first origin. Take a certain weight of gold or silver, still a rough mass: its collected habit is small, less for the time being than it will be, yet containing within the line of its measure all that is the nature of gold or silver. Then, when the mass is spread out into a sheet, it is made greater than its beginning, by the expansion of a fixed weight, not by addition, while it is extended, not while it is increased. Even so it is increased, while it is extended; for it may be increased in habit, though it may not in state. Then too the very splendour of the gold or silver is brought out, which had indeed been in the mass too, but more obscure — yet not none. Then too other and other habits accrue, according to the pliancy of the material, in whatever way he who works it shall draw it, conferring nothing on the measure but a shape. So too the increases of the soul are to be reckoned, not substantial, but evocative.

But although we have established beforehand that all the natural things of the soul are inherent in its very substance, pertaining to sense and intellect, and out of the inborn census of the soul, yet they come forth gradually through the spaces of age, and variously emerge through accidents, according to arts, to institutions, to places, to presiding powers — yet, to make for the now-proposed fellowship of flesh and soul, we say that the animal puberty too concurs with the carnal, and that the one rises up by the access of the senses, and the other by the advancement of the members, equally from about the fourteenth year — not because Asclepiades reckons wisdom from then, nor because the civil laws from this point apportion the management of affairs, but because this too is from the first origin a reasonable thing. For if Adam and Eve, from the knowledge of good and evil, felt the need to cover their shameful parts, then from the moment we feel this very thing, we profess the knowledge of good and evil. From these years, moreover, the sex is both more suffused and more clothed, and concupiscence uses the eyes as its arbiters and communicates its pleasure, and understands what things are, and girds its boundaries, after the likeness of the fig-leaf contagion, with itching, and leads man out of the paradise of integrity — thereafter scabbed even into the other faults, and into transgressions not natural, since now they are not from the institution of nature, but from vice. For the rest, properly natural concupiscence is one only, of foods alone, which God both conferred at the first origin: ‘Of every tree,’ He says, ‘you shall eat’; and measured out anew to the second generation after the flood: ‘Behold, I have given you all things for food, as the green herb of the grass’ — looking not so much to the soul as to the flesh, even though for the soul's sake. For the occasion of the arguer is to be taken away, who, because the soul seems to desire foods, from this too wishes it understood mortal, in that it is sustained by foods, and, in short, grows faint when they are taken away, and lastly perishes when they are withdrawn. But it is not only to be set forth who it is that desires them, but also for whom; and if for itself, then also why, and when, and how far; and that nature desires one thing, necessity another, the property of a thing one thing, the cause another. The soul therefore will desire foods — for itself indeed by reason of necessity, but for the flesh by the nature of property. For surely the flesh is the house of the soul, and the soul the inhabitant of the flesh. The inhabitant, then, will desire, by reason and by necessity of this name, things to profit the house through the whole time of its tenancy — not that it itself is to be underpinned, nor itself to be plastered, nor itself to be shored up, but only to be held together, since it cannot otherwise be held together than by a house upheld. Otherwise it will be permitted to the soul, when the house has fallen down through the failure of its proper supports, to depart unharmed, having its own firm foundations and the nourishments of its own condition — immortality, rationality, sensibility, intellectuality, freedom of will.

All which things conferred upon the soul at its birth, the same one who envied at the first origin now too overshadows and depraves, so that they may not either be voluntarily provided for or administered as they ought. For to which of men will the evil spirit not cleave, lying in wait for souls from the very gate of birth, since he is invited even by all that superstition of childbirth? So all are born under the midwifery of idolatry, while the very wombs, still bound about with fillets prepared before the idols, profess their offspring to be candidates of the demons; while in childbirth the wail is raised to Lucina and Diana; while throughout the whole hebdomad a table is set out for Juno; while on the last day the Fates of Writing are summoned; while even the first setting of the infant upon the ground is sacred to the goddess Statina. Who, thereafter, does not either vow the whole head of his son to guilt, or take off some lock, or shave it wholly with the razor, or bind it with a sacrifice, or seal it with a sacred rite — for a national, an ancestral, a public or a private devotion? So, then, the demonic spirit found Socrates too while still a boy. So to all men genii are assigned, which is a name of demons. So scarcely any birth is clean — at least among the heathen. Hence the apostle too says that holy children are procreated from a sanctified parent of either sex, as much from the prerogative of the seed as from the discipline of the institution. ‘Otherwise,’ he says, ‘they would be born unclean’ — wishing the children of the faithful to be understood as designated nevertheless for sanctity, and through this for salvation too, that by the pledge of this hope he might patronize the marriages which he had judged worthy of being retained. Otherwise he remembered the Lord's definition: ‘Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God’ — that is, he shall not be holy.

Thus every soul, up to that point, is reckoned in Adam until it is recounted in Christ; so long unclean as it is not recounted; but a sinner, because unclean, taking back its own ignominy onto the flesh too out of fellowship. For although the flesh is a sinner, according to which we are forbidden to walk, whose works of concupiscence against the spirit are condemned, and on whose account men are noted as carnal — yet the flesh is not infamous in its own name. For it neither of itself savours anything nor perceives, so as to persuade or command a fault. Why should it? being a ministry — and a ministry not such as a slave or a lesser friend, who are animate and men, but such as a cup, or some other thing of the kind: a body, not a soul. For the cup too is the ministry of the thirsty; yet unless he who thirsts has applied the cup to himself, the cup will minister nothing. So entirely is there no property of man in the earthy thing; nor is the flesh man, as though another power of the soul and another person, but it is a thing plainly of another substance and another condition, yet assigned to the soul as its furniture, as an instrument in the offices of life. The flesh, therefore, is upbraided in the Scriptures, because without the flesh the soul does nothing in the working of lust, gluttony, drunkenness, cruelty, idolatry, and the other carnal things — not the senses, but the effects. In short, the senses of faults are wont to be imputed to the soul even without the effects: ‘He who has looked to lust has already committed adultery in his heart.’ For the rest, what does the flesh do without the soul in the working of probity, justice, endurance, chastity? Moreover, what kind of thing is it that you should subscribe crimes to that to which you ascribe no proper good documents? But that through which the offence is committed is convened, that the soul, from which the offence proceeds, may be burdened — even in the accusation of the ministry. The graver odium is against the governor when his offices are assailed. He is the more punished who commands, when not even he who obeys is excused.

The evil of the soul, then, besides that which is built upon it from the access of the evil spirit, comes first from the fault of origin, being in a manner natural. For, as we said, the corruption of nature is another nature, having its own god and father, namely the very author of corruption — yet so that there is also in the soul that good which is principal, that divine and genuine and properly natural good. For that which is from God is not so much extinguished as overshadowed. For it can be overshadowed, because it is not God; it cannot be extinguished, because it is from God. And so, just as light hindered by some obstacle remains, but does not appear, if the density of the obstacle has been so great — so too the good in the soul, oppressed by the evil, according to its quality either is wholly idle, its light being hidden, or, where it is given, shines out, its liberty being found. So there are some men most evil and some best, and yet all souls are nonetheless of one kind. So even in the worst there is something of good, and in the best somewhat of the worst. For God alone is without sin, and the only man without sin is Christ, since Christ is also God. So too the divinity of the soul breaks forth into presages out of its prior good, and the consciousness of God comes forth into testimony: ‘God is good,’ and ‘God sees,’ and ‘I commend it to God.’ For this reason no soul is without crime, because none is without the seed of good. Accordingly, when it comes to the faith, reformed by the second nativity out of water and supernal power, the curtain of its former corruption drawn aside, it beholds its whole light. It is taken up too by the Holy Spirit, as in its former nativity by the profane spirit. The flesh follows the soul now wedded to the spirit, as a dowered chattel, and now no longer the handmaid of the soul, but of the spirit. O blessed wedlock, if it admit no adultery!

It remains now to treat of death, that the matter may there be set down where the soul itself comes to its consummation — although Epicurus, by a sufficiently vulgar opinion, has denied that death pertains to us. ‘For that which is dissolved,’ he says, ‘lacks sense, and what lacks sense is nothing to us.’ But it is not death itself that is dissolved and lacks sense, but the man who suffers it. Yet he assigned the suffering to that whose is the action. But if it belongs to man to suffer the death that dissolves the body and destroys sense, how absurd it is that so great a force should be said not to pertain to man! Much more forced is Seneca, who says, ‘After death all things are finished, even death itself.’ If this is so, then death too will pertain to itself, if it too is finished — and the more to man, in whom, among all things, by being finished, it too is finished. ‘Death is nothing to us’ — then life too is nothing to us. For if that by which we are dissolved is beyond us, then that too by which we are compacted is outside us. If the removal of sense is nothing to us, neither is the acquisition of sense anything to us. But let him who would do away with the soul do away with death too. By us, as concerning the posthumous life and the further province of the soul, so too death shall be treated of, to which we ourselves pertain, even if it does not pertain to us. In short, not even its mirror, sleep, is foreign matter.

Of sleep let us dispute first, and afterwards how the soul runs its course after death. Sleep is by no means beyond nature, as it pleases certain philosophers, since they reckon it from those two causes which are held to be outside nature. The Stoics affirm sleep to be a relaxation of the sensual vigour; the Epicureans, a diminution of the animal spirit; Anaxagoras, with Xenophanes, a weariness; Empedocles and Parmenides, a cooling; Strato, a segregation of the implanted spirit; Democritus, a want of spirit; Aristotle, a withering of the heat about the heart. I presume I have never so slept as to recognize any of these. For neither is it to be believed that sleep is weariness, but rather the contrary of weariness, which it takes away, since a man is by sleep more restored than wearied. Moreover, sleep is not always conceived out of weariness, and yet, when it is from weariness, the weariness is then no longer there. But neither will I admit a cooling or any withering of heat, since bodies grow so warm in sleep that the distribution of foods would not easily proceed through sleep — the heat being a quickener, the chill a delayer — if we were cooled by sleep. There is more: that the sweat too is the index of a boiling digestion. In short, we are said to ‘cook’ our food, which is the operation of heat, not of cold. Likewise the immortality of the soul does not allow us to believe in a diminution of the animal spirit, or a want of spirit, or a segregation of the implanted spirit. The soul perishes if it is lessened. It remains, perhaps, that with the Stoics we should determine sleep to be a relaxation of the sensual vigour, since it procures the rest of the body alone, not also of the soul. For the soul, as ever mobile and ever exercised, never sinks into rest, which is foreign to the state of immortality; for nothing immortal admits an end of its work, but sleep is an end of work. In short, to the body, to which mortality belongs, to it alone does rest flatter with an end of its work. Whoever, then, will doubt of the naturalness of sleep has indeed the dialecticians bringing the whole distinction of natural and beyond-natural into doubt, so that he may know that even what he has thought to be apart from nature can be claimed for the nature from which it has been so allotted that it seems to be held apart from her — and that surely either all things are by nature, or there is no nature at all. But among us that may be heard which the contemplation of God suggests, the author of all the things in question. For we believe that, if there is anything by nature, it is some rational work of God. Moreover, reason precedes sleep — sleep so apt, so useful, so necessary, that without it no soul would suffice — the restorer of bodies, the renewer of strength, the prover of health, the pacifier of toils, the physician of labours; to whose lawful enjoyment day gives way, night makes a law, taking away even the colour of things. But if sleep is vital, salutary, helpful, nothing of this kind is not rational, nothing not natural. So too the physicians relegate everything contrary to the vital, salutary, helpful, beyond the natural hinges. For even the maladies that rival sleep — the phrenetic and the cardiac — by judging them beyond nature, they have pre-judged natural sleep to be natural; even in lethargy, by noting it as not natural, they answer with a natural testimony, since sleep, in its own temperament, is natural. For all nature is cut off either by defrauding or by excess; it is preserved by the propriety of measure. Thus that will be natural in state which can be made not natural by deficiency or excess. What, if I should also except eating and drinking from the lots of nature? For in these too there is very much preparation of sleep. Certainly with these man was imbued from the first origin of his nature. If you learn it from God: that fount of the race, Adam, drank in slumber before he thirsted for rest, slept before he laboured, nay, before he even ate, nay, before he even spoke — that men may see that natural sleep, the index, is more principal than all natural things. Thence we are led to recognize that even then he was reviewing an image of death. For if Adam gave a figure of Christ, the sleep of Adam was the death of Christ, who was to sleep into death, so that out of the wound likewise of His side might be figured the true mother of the living, the Church. Therefore sleep too is so salutary, so rational, that it is fashioned even into a pattern of the now public and common death. For God willed — and elsewhere too has wrought nothing in His dispensation without exemplars, by the Platonic paradigm — to deal with us daily, more fully, the lines especially of man's beginning and end, stretching out His hand to faith, to be the more easily aided by images and parables, as of words, so of things too. He sets before you, then, a body struck down by the friendly force of slumber, prostrate by the soft necessity of rest, motionless in its posture, such as it lay before life, and such as it will lie after life, as an attestation of the modeling and of burial, awaiting the soul as not yet conferred, and as already snatched away. But it too so suffers as to seem to act elsewhere, learning, by the dissimulation of its presence, its future absence: about Hermotimus we shall know. And yet meanwhile it dreams. Whence then come dreams? It neither rests nor grows wholly idle, nor consigns the nature of its immortality to the holidays of slumber. It proves itself ever mobile; it journeys by land, by sea; it does business, is set in motion, labours, plays, grieves, rejoices, pursues things lawful and unlawful; it shows that it can do very much even without the body; that it is furnished too with its own members; but that nonetheless it has need again of the body to be set in motion. So, when the body has awakened, restored to its offices, it affirms to you the resurrection of the dead. This will be both the natural reason of sleep and the rational nature of it. Even by the image of death you are initiated into faith, you meditate hope, you learn to die and to live, you learn to be watchful while you sleep.

As for Hermotimus, his soul, as they say, was wanting in sleep, as though, by the occasion of the man being at leisure, it set out from the body. His wife disclosed this. His enemies, finding him asleep, burned him for dead. His soul, returning too late, imputed to itself, I believe, the homicide. The citizens of Clazomenae console Hermotimus with a temple. The woman does not approach it, on account of the disgrace of a wife. To what purpose this tale? That, since it is easy for the common crowd to suppose sleep to be a secession of the soul, credulity might not be suborned by this argument of Hermotimus too. It had been a case of somewhat heavier slumber, as is the presumption about the nightmare-spirit, or about that lapse of health which Soranus opposes, excluding the nightmare, or some such defect as drove even Epimenides into a fable, drowsy for nearly fifty years. But Suetonius too says that Nero, and Theopompus that Thrasymedes, never dreamed, save that Nero scarcely did, at his last end, after his terrors. What, if Hermotimus too was such that the leisure of a soul doing nothing in sleep was believed a divorce? You would conjecture anything rather than this licence of a soul running away without death, and indeed continually by its very form. For if such a thing were said to happen once, like an eclipse of the sun or moon, so too of the soul, I might fairly be persuaded that it was done divinely; for it is fitting that a man be either admonished or terrified by God, as by a swift lightning-flash, by the stroke of a momentary death — if it were not rather more in keeping to believe it a dream, which ought rather to befall one waking; if it ought not rather be believed a dream.

Here we are bound to bring forth a Christian opinion concerning dreams too, as concerning the accidents of sleep, but not light tossings of the soul, which we have declared busy and ever exercised out of the perpetuity of its motion, which is the very reason of its divinity and immortality. Therefore, when rest comes to bodies, whose proper solace it is, the soul, idle for any solace foreign to it, does not rest; and if it lacks the work of the corporeal members, it uses its own. Conceive a gladiator without arms, or a charioteer without his car, miming all the bearing and effort of his art: there is fighting, there is striving, but the tossing is empty.
