Nonetheless those things seem to be done which yet are not seen to be done; for they are done in act, but not done in effect. This force we call ecstasy, an excess of sense, and the likeness of madness. So too in the first origin sleep was dedicated together with ecstasy: ‘And God sent an ecstasy upon Adam, and he slept.’ For sleep came to the body for rest; ecstasy came upon the soul against rest; and thence already a form, mixing sleep with ecstasy, and a nature out of the form. In short, we are both delighted and saddened and terrified in dreams — how feelingly and anxiously and with what suffering — when in no waking matter we should be so moved, namely by empty images; whereas, if we dreamed in possession of ourselves, we should not. In short, good deeds too are gratuitous in dreams, and faults secure; for no more shall we be condemned for a vision of stuprum than crowned for one of martyrdom. ‘And how,’ you say, ‘is the soul mindful of its dreams, which is not permitted to be in possession of itself?’ This will be the property of this madness, that it does not come from the corruption of good health, but from the reason of nature; for it does not put the mind to flight, but draws it aside. It is one thing to shake, another to move; one thing to overturn, another to set in motion. Therefore, that the memory holds out, is the soundness of the mind; that the soundness of the mind, with the memory preserved, is stupefied, is a kind of madness. Therefore we are not said to rave, but to dream; therefore we are also prudent, if ever we are. For our wisdom, though it be overshadowed, is yet not extinguished — save that this too may seem to be idle then, while ecstasy works even this of its own property, that thus it brings before us the images of wisdom, just as also of error.

Behold, again we are pressed even by the retreatment of these very dreams by which the soul is tossed, to express ourselves. And when shall we come to death? Here too I would say, When God shall have granted; there are no long delays of that which is to come. Epicurus judged dreams wholly vain, freeing the divinity from business, and dissolving the order of things, and scattering all in passivity, as exposed to chance and fortuitous. But if it is so, then there will be also some outcome of truth, since it does not admit that this alone should be exempted from the chance owed to all. Homer divided two gates for dreams, the horn one of truth, the ivory one of falsehood. For one looks through horn, but ivory is opaque. Aristotle, ascribing to dreams a greater part of falsehood, yet acknowledges the true too. The Telmessians void no dreams, but accuse the weakness of the conjecture. But who is so foreign to humanity as not to have felt at some time some faithful vision? Touching upon a few of the more notable ones, I shall impose shame upon Epicurus. Herodotus relates that Astyages, king of the Medes, saw in a dream that the bladder of his daughter Mandane, still a virgin, flowed forth into a deluge of Asia; likewise, a year after her marriage, that out of the same parts a vine arose and overshadowed all Asia. This too Charon of Lampsacus, earlier than Herodotus, hands down. Those who interpreted her son for so great a work did not deceive themselves; since Cyrus both submerged and pressed down Asia. Philip of Macedon, not yet a father, had seen that he had sealed his wife Olympias' nature with a ring; the device was a lion. He had believed her generation closed (because, I suppose, the lion is a father only once); Aristodemus or Aristophon, conjecturing rather that nothing empty is sealed, that a son was portended, and indeed one of the greatest impetus. Those who know Alexander recognize the lion of the ring. Ephorus writes it. But Dionysius' tyranny over Sicily a certain woman of Himera dreamed too. Heraclides has reported it. And to Seleucus the kingdom of Asia, his mother Laodice foresaw, before she had borne him. Euphorion published it. Mithridates too, from a dream, I learn from Strabo, took possession of Pontus; and that Baralis the Illyrian ruled from the Molossians as far as Macedonia, from a dream, I learn from Callisthenes. The Romans too have known dreams of this kind of truth. The reformer of the empire, still a little boy and private in station, and only Julius Octavius, and unknown to himself, Marcus Tullius knew from a dream as both Augustus and the burier of the civil whirlwinds. It is recorded in the commentaries of Vitellius. Nor will this be the only species, the herald of the highest powers, but also of perils and of destructions: as when Caesar, otherwise ill, in the battle of his enemies Brutus and Cassius at Philippi, yet thinking he would bring back a greater danger from the foe, escaped, by a vision shown to Artorius, leaving the tent; as when his daughter foresaw a cross for Polycrates of Samos, from the anointing of the sun and the washing of Jupiter. Honours too and talents are revealed through sleep, remedies too are furnished, thefts too are betrayed, treasures too are conferred. Cicero's dignity, while he was still a little one, his nurse had already beheld. The swan from the bosom of Socrates, soothing men, is the disciple Plato. Leonymus the boxer is healed by Achilles in dreams. When the people of Athens had lost a golden crown from the citadel, the tragedian Sophocles by dreaming found it again. The tragic actor Neoptolemus, near Rhoeteum the burial-place of Troy, warned in dreams by Ajax himself, frees his tomb from ruin, and, when he puts down the rubbish of the stones, returns thence rich with gold. How many commentators and affirmers there are on this matter! Artemon, Antiphon, Strato, Philochorus, Epicharmus, Serapion, Cratippus and Dionysius the Rhodian, Hermippus, the whole literature of the age. The only one I shall perhaps laugh at is he who thought to persuade us that Saturn dreamed before all others; unless Aristotle too lived before all others, forgive me for laughing. For the rest, Epicharmus, with Philochorus the Athenian, even raised dreams to the highest summit among the kinds of divination. For the world too is crowded with oracles of this kind — as of Amphiaraus at Oropus, of Amphilochus at Mallus, of Sarpedon in the Troad, of Trophonius in Boeotia, of Mopsus in Cilicia, of Hermione in Macedonia, of Pasiphae in Laconia. The rest, with their origins and rites and reporters, together with the whole history of dreams thereafter, Hermippus of Berytus will most abundantly exhibit in five volumes. But the Stoics too prefer to hold that God, most provident of human instruction, among other helps of the divining arts and disciplines, implanted dreams too in us, the peculiar solace of a natural oracle. So much as to the faith of dreams, which is to be sealed by us too, but interpreted otherwise. For as to the other oracles too, where no one sleeps, what else shall we pronounce than that their account is demonic — of those spirits which dwelt even then in the very men, or affected their memories, for every scene of their malice — feigning divinity in this kind too, and by the same industry deceiving even through benefits of medicines and admonitions and predictions, that they may the more hurt by helping, while through the things by which they help they lead men away from the inquiry into the true divinity by the insinuation of the false? And surely this power is not shut up, nor circumscribed by the bounds of shrines; it is wandering and flying about and meanwhile free. So that no one will doubt that houses too lie open to demons, and that they beset men with images, not only in shrines but in bedchambers.

For we define that dreams are for the most part struck in upon us by demons — even though sometimes true and gracious, but, by that industry of which we have spoken, affecting and ensnaring — how much more often vain and frustrating and turbid and mocking and unclean! Nor is it any wonder if the images are theirs whose the realities too are. But from God — who has promised, namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit upon all flesh, and that as His servants and handmaids should prophesy, so should they dream — those will be reckoned which are compared to that very grace: if any be honourable, holy, prophetic, revelatory, edifying, vocatory; whose liberality is wont to distil even upon the profane, since God too levels His rains and His suns equally upon the just and the unjust — seeing that Nebuchadnezzar too dreamed by divine appointment, and nearly the greater number of men learn God out of visions. As, therefore, there is the deigning of God even toward the heathen, so is there the temptation of the evil one toward the saints, from whom he does not desist even by day, so as to creep upon them sleeping as he can, if upon them waking he cannot. The third species will be dreams which the soul seems to bring upon itself out of the intentness of its surrounding circumstances. But since it is not in our choice to dream (for Epicharmus too thinks thus), how will the soul itself be to itself the cause of any vision? Is then this species to be left to the natural form, which preserves to the soul, even in ecstasy, the experiencing of its own things? But those which seem to befall neither from God nor from a demon nor from the soul — beyond opinion and beyond interpretation and beyond the power of narration — these will be set apart for ecstasy properly and its own reason.

They affirm that more certain and more refined things are dreamed in the last watches of the night, as if then the vigour of souls were emerging, the slumber being now drawn forth. As to the seasons of the year, that the spring is the more quiet, because summer dissolves the souls, and winter in some manner hardens them, and autumn, otherwise a tempter of healths, dilutes them with the most vinous juices of fruits. Likewise, as to the very posture of rest, that if one lie neither supine nor on the right side, nor with the inward parts thrown back, as if the cells were overflowed, the station of the senses may float, or the seat of the mind be choked by a compressed quinsy of the liver. But I should think these things ingeniously estimated rather than firmly proved (although it is Plato who estimated them); and perhaps they proceed by chance. Otherwise dreams will be in our choice, if they can be directed. For as to the fact that now presumption, now superstition, prescribes a discipline for dreams by the distinguishing or denying of foods, it is to be examined. Superstition, as when at the oracles a fast is enjoined upon those about to sleep there, that it may induce a chastity; presumption, as when the Pythagoreans, on this account too, reject the bean, a burdensome and flatulent food. But on the other hand, that fraternity of three with Daniel, content with pulse alone, lest they should be defiled by the royal dishes, redeemed from God, besides the rest of their wisdom, especially the grace of dreams, both of obtaining and of expounding them. As for fasts, I know not whether I alone, for the most part, so dream that I do not perceive that I have dreamed. ‘Then is sobriety nothing,’ you say, ‘to this part?’ Nay, the more to this in proportion as it is to all; if to superstition, much more to religion. For so even the demons demand it of their dreamers, namely for the pandering of divinity, since they know the friend of God — since Daniel too, again, by a station of three weeks grew dry in his diet, but in order to allure God by the offices of humiliation, not in order to build up sense and wisdom for the soul about to dream, as though it would not act in ecstasy. So sobriety will profit not for removing ecstasy, but for commending the very ecstasy, that it may come about in God.

Those who think infants do not dream, since all the powers of the soul are discharged according to the measure of age in life, let them observe their startings and noddings and smilings in sleep, that from the fact they may grasp that the motions of the dreaming soul easily break out to the surface through the tenderness of the flesh. But also, that the Libyan nation of the Atlantes is said to pass the night in a blind sleep, is assuredly charged to the nature of the soul. For either fame lied to Herodotus, sometimes slanderous against barbarians, or a great force of demons of this kind dominates in that climate. For if Aristotle too notes a certain hero of Sardinia who deprives the sleepers in his fane of their visions, this too will be among the wantonness of demons, as much to take away dreams as to bring them in, so that the mark of Nero too, a late dreamer, and of Thrasymedes proceeded thence. But we deduce dreams from God too. Why then would not the Atlantes dream even from God — or because no nation is now a stranger to God, the Gospel coruscating into all the earth and unto the bounds of the world? Did then either fame lie to Aristotle, or is there still the reckoning of demons — provided that no nature of soul be believed exempt from dreams?

Enough concerning the mirror of death, that is, sleep; and then concerning the businesses of sleep, that is, dreams. Now to the origin of this digression, that is, to the order of death — since not even this is without questions, although it is the end of all questions. By the public verdict of the whole human race, we pronounce death the debt of nature. This the voice of God stipulated, this everything that is born has promised; that even from this point Epicurus' stupor may not be poured over us, denying that this debt pertains to us, but rather the madness of the heretic Menander the Samaritan may be spat upon, who says that death not only does not pertain to his followers, but does not even reach them. To wit, he is sent as a legate from a supernal and hidden power, that those who shall have put on his baptism may become immortal and incorruptible and at once partakers of the resurrection. We read indeed of very many wonderful kinds of waters: as the wine-bearing vein of the Lyncestae renders men drunken; as the demonic spring of Colophon makes them frantic; as the poisoned water of Nonacris in Arcadia befell Alexander. There was too in Judaea a healing lake before Christ. The poet plainly handed down the Stygian marsh as washing away death. But Thetis too bewailed her son. And although Menander too plunges men into the Styx, one will have to die nonetheless, that one may come to the Styx; for it is said to be among the dead. What and where is that happiness of waters which neither John the Baptist administered nor Christ Himself showed to His disciples? What is this bath of Menander? A comic one, I believe. But why so infrequent, so hidden, where the fewest wash? For I shall make so great a rarity suspect of a most secure and safe sacrament — at which there is not even a law to die for God Himself, when, on the contrary, all nations now go up into the mountain of the Lord and into the house of the God of Jacob, who demands death even through martyrdom, which He exacted even of His own Christ. Nor will anyone grant so much to magic that it should exempt from death, or re-dig life like a vine renewed in age. For this was not permitted even to Medea upon a man, though it was permitted upon a ram. Enoch was translated, and Elias, nor was their delay found — postponed, namely. For the rest, being to die, they are reserved, that they may extinguish the antichrist with their blood. John too died, of whom the hope had been in vain that he would remain until the coming of the Lord. For heresies generally spring up after our examples, taking thence the supports from which they fight. Lastly, this is the short way: Where are those whom Menander himself drenched, whom he plunged into his Styx? Let the apostles come, abiding for ever, and stand by. Let my Thomas see them, hear, handle — and he believed.

But the work of death is in the midst — the separation of body and soul. But some, to defend the immortality of the soul, which indeed, not taught by God, they uphold feebly, so beg their argumentations that they would have it believed that even after death certain souls cleave to bodies. For to this end Plato too, although he dispatches what souls he will to heaven straightway, yet in the Republic opposes the corpse of a certain unburied man preserved a long time without any decay — on account, namely, of the indivisibility of the soul. To this end too Democritus notes the growths of nails and hair in the graves for some space of time. Yet the quality of the air too could have been a protection to that body. For what, if the air were drier and the soil saltier? what, if the very substance of the body were more juiceless? what, if the very kind of death had already discharged the corrupting materials beforehand? But the nails, since they are the beginnings of the sinews, are with reason seen to be pushed out further, the sinews being stretched out by relaxation, and the flesh failing daily; the hairs too have their nourishment from the brain, which a hidden protection grants to last for a while. In short, even in the living, according to the richness of the brain, the head of hair either flows or deserts. You have the physicians. But neither is it the case that a little of the soul subsides in the body, destined to depart at some time itself too, when time shall have abolished the whole scene of the body. For this too is in the opinion of certain men. Therefore they say that the dead are not to be buried by fire, sparing the superfluous part of the soul. But there is another reason for this piety, not flattering the relics of the soul, but abhorring cruelty even in the name of the body, which too man assuredly does not deserve to have spent in a penal end. For the rest, the soul, being indivisible, as immortal, demands that even death be believed indivisible — befalling indivisibly, not as to an immortal, but as to an indivisible soul. But death too will be divided, if the soul too is, by the superfluous part, namely, of the soul that is some time to die. So a portion of death will remain with a portion of the soul. Nor am I ignorant that there is some trace of this opinion. From my own experience I have learned it. I know a certain woman, a native daughter of the Church, of unimpaired form and age, deceased after a single and brief marriage; who, when she had slept in peace, and while the burial was still delayed, was meanwhile being composed by the prayer of a presbyter — at the first breath of the prayer she removed her hands from her sides into the posture of a suppliant, and, the peace being again said, restored them to their station. There is too that report among our own people, that a body, set side by side with another in the cemetery, made room by withdrawal for the new-comer. And if among the heathen too any such thing is handed down, everywhere God sets forth signs of His power, for solace to His own, for testimony to strangers. For I would rather believe a thing done in testimony from God than from any relics of the soul; which, if they were there, would have moved the other members too; and if the hands only, yet not for the cause of prayer. That body too would not only have yielded to a brother, but otherwise too, by a change of posture, would have eased itself. Certainly, whencesoever these things are, they are rather to be reckoned signs and portents; they cannot establish a natural law. Death, if it is not at once wholly death, is not death. If anything of the soul remain, it is life. Death will no more be mingled with life than night with day.

This work of death, then — the separation of flesh and soul — human feeling has distinguished in two ways, setting aside the question of fates and fortuitous things: into an ordinary and an extraordinary form; the ordinary indeed reckoning to nature, of any quiet death, but judging the extraordinary contrary to nature, of any violent end. But we, who know the first origins of man, boldly determine that death did not follow man from nature, but from fault, which is not itself even natural — though the name of nature is easily usurped for those things which seem to have cleaved from birth out of accident. For if man had been directly instituted unto death, then at last death would be ascribed to nature. But the law itself proves that he was not instituted unto death, suspending it by a conditional threat, and assigning the event of death to the choice of man. In short, if he had not sinned, he would by no means have died. So that will not be nature which befalls from the power of an option through the will, not from the authority of the institution through necessity. Accordingly, even though the exits of death are various, as the condition of causes is manifold, we call none so gentle that it is not wrought by force. That very operative reason of death, though simple, is a force. For what? since it tears asunder and divides so great a fellowship of soul and flesh, so great a coalescence of the sister substances from conception. For even though a man should breathe out his spirit for joy, as Chilon the Spartan, while embracing his son the victor at Olympia; even though for glory, as Clidemus the Athenian, while crowned with gold for the excellence of his historical style; even though through a dream, as Plato; even though through laughter, as Publius Crassus — much more violent is the death which makes its way through good things, which expels the soul through favourable circumstances, which brings death then when it is more pleasant to live, in exultation, in honour, in repose, in pleasure. There is force in the case of ships, when, far from the rocks of Caphareus, beaten by no whirlwinds, shaken by no great waves, with a flattering breeze, with a gliding course, with a rejoicing crew, they sink down suddenly by an inward shock with all their security. Not otherwise are the shipwrecks of life, even the outcome of a tranquil death. It makes no difference whether the ship of the body departs entire or shattered, so long as the soul's voyage is overthrown.

But whither then will the soul, naked and ejected, turn aside? Without doubt we shall follow it out in order. Yet first I shall fill up what belongs to this place, lest, because we have spoken of the various exits of death, anyone should expect from us the reasons of each — to be left rather to the physicians, the proper arbiters of all lethal things or causes, and of the very corporeal conditions. Plainly, to protect here too the immortality of the soul, in mentioning death I shall interpose somewhat concerning that kind of exit in which the soul slips away little by little and bit by bit; for, sustaining the habit of failing, it is led off while it seems to be consumed, and offers a conjecture of perishing out of the temper of its excess. But the whole account is in the body and out of the body. For whatever that exit of death be, without doubt it is the overthrow either of the materials or of the regions or of the vital ways: of the materials, as of the bile, as of the blood; of the regions, as of the heart, as of the liver; of the ways, as of the veins, as of the arteries. While, then, these are laid waste in the body, each from its own cause of injury, even to the last overthrow and rescission of the vital things — that is, of the natural boundaries, seats, offices — necessarily the soul too, its instruments and dwellings and spaces gradually slipping away, is itself too gradually compelled to migrate, and is led off into the appearance of diminution, in no other manner than as the charioteer too is presumed to have failed when the exhaustion of his horses has denied their strength — as to the disposition of the man left destitute, not as to the truth of suffering. Just so the charioteer of the body, the animal spirit, fails in the name of the failing vehicle, not in his own — withdrawing from work, not from vigour; languishing in act, not in state; boiling away his constancy, not his substance, because he ceases to appear, not because he ceases to be. So too every swift death, as the harvest of necks, opening at once and so great a gate, as the force of a ruin dashing out all the vital things at once, as apoplexy, an inner ruin — affords no delay to the soul, nor racks its departure into moments. But where the death is long, as the soul is deserted, so it deserts; yet it is not cut down in this fashion, but drawn out; and while it is drawn out, it makes its last part seem its whole. Not every part, however, is at once severed too, because it is the last, nor, because it is small, is it at once itself too about to perish. Its own end follows in the series, and the middle part is drawn to the summit, and the remnants, cohering with the whole, are awaited by it, not deserted. And so I would dare to say that the last of the whole is the whole, since, though it be less and posterior, it is the soul's own. Hence, in short, it often happens that the soul, in the very divorce, is more powerfully set in motion, with more anxious gaze, with extraordinary loquacity — since, established now from a greater eminence in liberty, through the superfluous part that still lingers in the body, it announces what it sees, what it hears, what it begins to know. For if this body is, by the Platonic verdict, a prison, but by the apostolic the temple of God, when one is in Christ, yet meanwhile it blocks up the soul within its enclosure, and overshadows it, and befouls it by the coalescence of the flesh — whence to it, as through a horn window, the light of things is the more obscured. Without doubt, when by the force of death it is squeezed out of the coalescence of the flesh, and by the very squeezing is strained clear, certainly it bursts out of the curtain of the body into the open, to its own pure and clear and proper light; at once it recognizes itself in the freeing of its substance, and recovers its divinity by its very liberty, as one emerging from sleep, from images to truths. Then too it announces what it sees, then it exults or trembles, according as it perceives the equipment of its lodging — from the very face at once of the angel, the summoner of souls, the Mercury of the poets.

Whither, then, the soul is conducted, we now render. Nearly all the philosophers who, in whatever fashion they will, yet vindicate the immortality of the soul — as Pythagoras, as Empedocles, as Plato — and those who grant it some time from its departure until the conflagration of the universe, as the Stoics, place their own souls alone — that is, those of the wise — in the supernal mansions. Plato indeed does not rashly grant this to the souls of philosophers, but to those of such as have, namely, adorned philosophy with the love of boys. So great a privilege, even among philosophers, has impurity. And so, with him, the wise souls are exalted into the ether; with Arius, into the air; with the Stoics, beneath the moon. At whom indeed I wonder that they prostrate the unwise souls about the earth, since they affirm that these are taught by the wise far above them. Where will be the region of the school, in so great a distance of lodgings? By what reason will the disciple-souls assemble to the mistress-souls, absent from each other by so great an interval? And what use and fruit of this posthumous instruction to them, who are at the very point of perishing in the conflagration? The rest of the souls they cast down to the lower regions. These Plato describes, in the Phaedo, as a kind of lap of the earth, whither all the dregs of worldly defilements, flowing together and there settling, breathe out, and, as out of the mire of their own uncleannesses, pack together there a grosser draught and a separate air.

But to us the lower regions are believed to be not a bare hollow, nor some sewer of the world open to the sky, but a vast space in the pit of the earth, and a depth hidden away in its very bowels — since we read that Christ accomplished a three days' death in the heart of the earth, that is, in the innermost and inner recess, covered within the earth itself and shut up within it, and built over by yet lower abysses. But if Christ, God though He be, because man too, died according to the Scriptures and was buried according to the same, satisfied this law also, having undergone in the lower regions the form of human death, nor ascended into the heights of the heavens before He descended into the lower parts of the earth, that there He might make the patriarchs and prophets partakers of Himself — then you have ground both to believe that the region of the lower world is subterranean, and to thrust away with your elbow those who too proudly think the souls of the faithful unworthy of the lower regions: servants above their Lord, and disciples above their Master, scorning, it may be, to receive in the bosom of Abraham the solace of awaiting the resurrection. ‘But for this,’ they say, ‘Christ went to the lower regions, that we should not go.’ For the rest, what difference is there between heathen and Christians, if the prison be the same for the dead? How then will the soul breathe up to heaven, while Christ still sits there at the right hand of the Father, the trumpet of the archangel not yet heard at God's command, those whom the Lord's coming shall find in the world not yet caught up to meet Him in the air, with those who, dead in Christ, shall rise first? To no one is heaven open, while earth is still safe, not to say closed. For with the passing of the world the kingdoms of the heavens will be unbarred. But our slumber, you say, is in the ether with the boy-lovers of Plato, or in the air with Arius, or about the moon with the Endymions of the Stoics. Nay, you say, in paradise, whither even then both patriarchs and prophets, the appendages of the Lord's resurrection, migrated from the lower regions. And how is it that the region of paradise, revealed to John in the Spirit, which lies beneath the altar, showed no other souls with it save those of the martyrs? How is it that Perpetua, that most valiant martyr, on the day of her passion, in a revelation of paradise, saw there only her fellow-martyrs — unless because to none does the sword, the doorkeeper of paradise, give way, save those who have died in Christ, not in Adam? A new death for God, and an extraordinary one for Christ, is received into another and a private lodging. Recognize, then, the difference between the heathen and the faithful in death, if you die for God, as the Paraclete admonishes, not in soft fevers and in little beds, but in martyrdoms; if you take up your cross and follow the Lord, as He Himself commanded. The whole key of paradise is your blood. You have too, from us, a little book concerning paradise, in which we have established that every soul is sequestered in the lower regions until the day of the Lord.

A debate presents itself: whether this is done at once from the departure, or whether some reason detains certain souls here in the meantime, or whether even those already received may afterwards intervene from the lower regions, by choice or by command. For persuasions for these opinions are not lacking. It has been believed that the unburied are not brought down to the lower regions before they have received their due rites — according to the Homeric Patroclus, demanding his funeral in dreams of Achilles, because he could not otherwise approach the gates of the lower world, the souls of the buried keeping him afar. But we know, besides the poetic rights, the industry too of Homer's piety. For he the more carefully placed the care of burial, in that he charged its delay as an injury to the souls; and at the same time, that no one, by detaining the dead at home, should himself be the more consumed with him by an excess of solace fed by grief. So he framed the complaints of the unburied soul to both ends, that both the urgency of the funeral and the honour of the bodies might be preserved, and the memory of the affections tempered. For the rest, how vain is it that the soul should await the rites of the body, as though it carried off thence anything to the lower regions! Much vainer, if the cessation of burial is to be reckoned an injury to the soul, which it ought rather to embrace as a favour. For surely it would prefer to be drawn off to the lower regions more slowly, which was unwilling to die at all. It will love an impious heir, through whom it is still fed by the light. Or if there is for certain some injury in being thrust beneath the earth more slowly, but the title of the injury is the cessation of burial, it is most unjust that it should be afflicted with an injury which will not be imputed to it — pertaining, namely, to its kindred. They say too that souls forestalled by an untimely death wander here until the remainder of their ages is completed — as long as they would have lived, had they not died out of season. Now either fixed times are appointed to each, and I shall not believe that the appointed times can be snatched away; or, if they are indeed appointed, but are mutilated by the will of God or some power, in vain are they mutilated, if they are still to be fulfilled. Or if they are not appointed, there will be no remainder of times not appointed. Further I shall add. Behold, an infant, say, has died beneath the founts of the breast; suppose now a beardless boy, suppose a youth coming of age, who yet would have lived eighty years — what kind of thing is it that the soul should pass these snatched-away years here after death? For age it cannot take on without a body, since ages are wrought through bodies. But let our own people too reconsider this, that souls are to receive again at the resurrection the same bodies in which they died. The same measures of bodies, then, are to be hoped for, and the same ages, which make the measures of the bodies. By what compact, then, can an infant's soul pass here the snatched-away times, so as to rise again at eighty in a body of one month? Or if it shall here be necessary for those times to be fulfilled which had been destined, will the soul also run through here, equally, the order of life which the times, equally destined here with them, had allotted — so that it should both study, being consigned from infancy to childhood, and serve as a soldier, being roused from adolescence to youth, and hold property, being weighted from youth to old age, and exact usury, and press the field, and sail, and go to law, and marry, and labour, and undergo sicknesses, and whatever sad and glad things awaited it along with the times? But these things, without a body, how shall they be transacted? life without life? But the times will be empty, to be filled up by their mere passage. What then hinders them from being fulfilled in the lower regions, where likewise there is no use of them? So we say that every soul, at whatever age it has deceased, abides in that age until that day on which the perfect thing is promised, tempered to the measure of angelic fullness. Accordingly, those will be held exiles from the lower regions whom they think to have been snatched away by violence, especially through the atrocities of punishments — I mean of the cross and the axe and the sword and the beast; nor, further, are those exits violent which justice decrees, the avenger of violence. ‘And therefore,’ you will say, ‘the wicked souls are exiled to the lower regions.’ Then I compel you to set up one of two things: either good lower regions, or evil. If you choose evil, then even now the worst souls ought to be hurled down thither; if good, why do you judge the souls of the immature and the unwedded, pure and innocent according to the condition of their age, meanwhile unworthy of the lower regions?

Either it is best to be detained here, according to the ‘aori,’ or worst, according to the ‘biaeothanatoi’ — that I may use the very words by which magic, the authoress of these opinions, sounds: Ostanes and Typhon and Dardanus and Damigeron and Nectabis and Berenice. There is now a public literature which promises that it will summon up, from the dwelling of the lower world, even souls laid to rest at a lawful age, even disjoined by an upright death, even discharged with prompt burial. What then shall we call magic? What nearly all do: a deception. But the reason of the deception escapes the Christians alone, who know the spirits of wickedness — not by an allied consciousness, but by a hostile knowledge — and handle, not by inviting operation but by an expugnatory dominion, that multiform plague of the human mind, the artificer of all error, the waster alike of salvation and of the soul. So too in magic — that is, in the second idolatry, in which the demons feign themselves dead in the same way as in the former they feign themselves gods (why not, since the gods too are dead?) — the ‘aori’ and the ‘biaeothanatoi’ are likewise invoked, under that argument of faith, that it should seem credible that those souls especially do violence and injury whom a savage and untimely end has wrung out by violence and injury, as though by way of requital for the offence. But the demons operate under cover of them, and these above all who were in those very persons when they were alive, and who had thrust them into ends of this kind. For we have suggested too that scarcely any man is free of a demon; and it is known to many that even immature and atrocious deaths are wrought by the operations of the demons, which they ascribe to onsets. This deception too, of the evil spirit lurking under the persons of the dead, we prove, unless I am mistaken, even by facts, since in exorcisms it sometimes affirms itself to be one of the parents of its man, sometimes a gladiator or a beast-fighter, just as elsewhere it affirms itself to be a god — caring for nothing more than this very thing, to exclude what we proclaim, lest we should easily believe that all souls are brought down to the lower regions, that it may disturb our faith both in judgment and in resurrection. And yet that demon, after he has tried to circumvent the bystanders, overcome by the urgency of divine grace, unwillingly confesses what is in the truth. So too in that other species of magic, which is believed to pluck up souls now at rest from the lower regions and exhibit them to view, there is no other more operative force of deception. Plainly, because a phantom is furnished, because a body too is feigned; nor is it any great matter for it to circumvent the outward eyes of one whose inner sharpness of mind it is most easy to blind. Bodies, in short, the dragons of the magical wands seemed to Pharaoh and the Egyptians. But the truth of Moses devoured the lie. Many things assuredly even against the apostles did Simon and Elymas the magi; but the stroke of blindness was not from their juggleries. What new thing is the rivalry of truth by an unclean spirit? Behold, today the heretics of this same Simon are exalted by so great a presumption of their art that they undertake even to move up the souls of the prophets from the lower regions. And I believe they can — by a lie. For not even to the Pythonic spirit then was it less permitted to feign the soul of Samuel, when Saul consulted the dead after God. Far be it otherwise that we should believe the soul of any saint, let alone of a prophet, to be drawn forth by a demon — taught as we are that Satan himself transfigures himself into an angel of light, let alone into a man of light, being even about to assert himself God at the end, and to put forth more portentous signs to overthrow, if it could be, the elect. He hesitated not, it may be, then to assert himself a prophet of God — and indeed to Saul, in whom he himself now lodged. Do not suppose that it was one who administered the phantom, and another who commended it, but that it was the same spirit both in the false prophetess and in the apostate, easily lying that he had made it be believed, through whom Saul's treasure was there where his heart too was — where, namely, God was not. And therefore, through whom he believed he would see, he saw, because through whom he saw, he also believed. And if it be objected, concerning the nocturnal images, that the dead are often seen not in vain (for the Nasamones, by lingering at the tombs of their parents, catch their own oracles, as Heraclides or Nymphodorus or Herodotus writes; and the Celts, for the same cause, pass the night at the barrows of brave men, as Nicander affirms) — we no more truly suffer the dead in dreams than the living; but by the same reason the dead as the living, and all things that are seen. For things are not true because they are seen, but because they are fulfilled. The faith of dreams is reported from the effect, not from the sight. That to no soul whatever do the lower regions lie open, the Lord sufficiently sanctioned in that argument of the poor man reposing and the rich man groaning, in the person of Abraham, that no reporter of the infernal disposition could be sent back thence — which even then might have been permitted, that Moses and the prophets might be believed. But even though God's power has recalled certain souls into bodies, in proof of His own right, it will not on that account be shared with the faith and audacity of magicians, and the deception of dreams, and the licence of the poets. Nay, in the examples of resurrection, when the power of God, whether through the prophets, or through Christ, or through the apostles, represents souls into bodies, it has been pre-judged, by a solid and handleable and satisfying truth, that this is the form of truth — so that you should judge every incorporeal exhibition of the dead a jugglery.

‘All souls, then, are in the keeping of the lower regions?’ you say. Will you or no, there are both punishments already there and refreshments; you have the poor man and the rich. And because I have deferred something or other to this part, I shall now opportunely render it in the conclusion. For why should you not think that the soul is both punished and cherished in the lower regions, meanwhile, under the expectation of either judgment, in a certain anticipation, and indeed a foretaste, of it? ‘Because,’ you say, ‘its business ought to be kept safe in the divine judgment, without any prelibation of the sentence; and then, because the restitution of the flesh too must be awaited, as the partner of its works and of its wages.’ What then shall come to pass in that time? Shall we sleep? But souls do not sleep even in the living; for sleep belongs to bodies, whose is death too, with its own mirror, sleep. Or will you have nothing done there, whither the whole of humanity is drawn, whither all hope is sequestered? Do you think judgment is foretasted, or begun? hurried on, or pre-administered? But indeed how most unjust it would be, even in the lower regions, if it goes well even there as yet with the guilty, and not yet with the innocent! What more would you have — that after death hope should be confused, and mocking us with an uncertain expectation, or that the review of life and the ordering of judgment should already be shuddered at? But does the soul always await the body, in order to grieve or to rejoice? Is it not of itself sufficient to itself for either title of feeling? How often, the body being unhurt, is the soul alone tormented by bile, by anger, by weariness, and most often unknown even to itself? How often, likewise, the body being afflicted, does the soul seek for itself a stolen joy, and withdraw then from the importunate fellowship of the body? I lie, if she is not wont, even out of the very torments of the body, to glory and rejoice alone. Look to the soul of Mucius, when he loosened his right hand in the fire; look to that of Zeno, when the torments of Dionysius passed him by. The bites of beasts are the ornaments of youth, as the scars of the bear in Cyrus. So fully does the soul know, even in the lower regions, both to rejoice and to grieve without the flesh; since both in the flesh, even unhurt, it grieves if it will, and, hurt, it rejoices if it will. If this be by its own choice in life, how much more by the judgment of God after death! But neither does the soul share all its works with the ministry of the flesh; for the divine censure pursues even mere thoughts and bare wills. ‘He who has looked to lust has already committed adultery in his heart.’ Therefore, even on this account, it is most fitting that the soul, even though the flesh be not awaited, should be punished for what, without the flesh's partnership, it committed. So too, for pious and benevolent thoughts, in which it had no need of the flesh, it shall be refreshed without the flesh. Nay, what if in carnal matters too it is the first which conceives, which arranges, which commands, which impels? And if ever unwilling, yet it first handles what it is to do through the body. Never, in short, will the conscience be later than the deed. So to this order too it answers that she should first weigh out the wages to whom they are first owed. In sum, when we understand that prison which the Gospel sets forth to be the lower regions, and interpret the last farthing to be even the smallest fault to be expiated there by the delay of the resurrection, no one will doubt that the soul pays back something in the keeping of the lower regions, the fullness of the resurrection being preserved through the flesh too. This too the Paraclete has most frequently commended, if anyone shall have admitted his discourses out of the acknowledgment of the promised gifts. To every human opinion concerning the soul, as I think, having engaged from the doctrine of faith, we have satisfied a curiosity at least just and necessary. But to one immense and idle there will be lacking as much to learn as it shall have pleased to inquire.
